slides.title: What SSRF is
slides.summary: The attacker makes your server fetch a URL of their choice, reaching systems only your server can see.
body: Features like “import from URL”, link previews, webhooks, PDF renderers and image proxies make a server fetch a URL the user supplies. In SSRF, the attacker points that URL inwards:

ul: http://169.254.169.254/: the cloud metadata service, which can hand out credentials;

body: It matters to frontend engineers because SSR servers, BFFs, edge functions and Next.js/Angular image optimisers all fetch URLs, often built from request data.
<mark>Your server is inside the network. An SSRF bug lets an outsider borrow that position.</mark>

steps.caption: The app fetches a URL to show its title and image.

item.label: Server fetches it
item.sub: The request comes from inside the cloud network

steps.caption: Firewalls don't stop requests from your own server.

item.label: Credentials leak
item.sub: The response is shown back as the “preview”

figure.alt: On the left, on the internet, an attacker cannot reach internal systems directly: a firewall blocks them. Instead they call your link-preview endpoint with url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/. Your server, inside the private network, fetches that URL. From there it can reach the cloud metadata service, which can return credentials, an internal admin panel at 10.0.0.5 and a Redis database on localhost. The response comes back to the attacker as the "preview".

slides.title: Defending against SSRF
slides.summary: Allowlist destinations, resolve and check IPs, re-check redirects, and isolate the fetcher.

ul: Allowlist hosts when you can (e.g. only your image CDN).
Resolve DNS and check the IP isn't private, loopback or link-local, then connect to that exact IP, so DNS rebinding can't swap it.
Re-check every redirect, or turn redirects off.
Isolate the fetcher in a network segment with no route to internal services, and require IMDSv2 on AWS.

body.note: Blocking the string “localhost” isn't enough: 127.1, [::1], decimal IPs like 2130706433, and DNS names that resolve to internal addresses all get around it.

body.more: The browser version: Local Network Access
body.text: Browsers have the same problem in reverse: a public website asking the user's browser to call their router or a local dev server. Since Chrome 142, a public site must get the user's permission before making requests to local network or loopback addresses.
